x.ASV: An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter into the assembly of Jehovah; even to the tenth generation shall none belonging to them enter into the assembly of Jehovah for ever:

nt: Moses says **until forever** as an extreme statement for emphasis. In this context, it does not mean literally “for eternity” but rather refers to an indeterminate future time, specifically for ten generations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [for all generations to come] or [permanently]

x.ASV: because they met you not with bread and with water in the way, when ye came forth out of Egypt, and because they hired against thee Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse thee.
x.Darby: because they met you not with bread and with water on the way, when ye came forth out of Egypt, and because they hired against thee Balaam the son of Beor, of Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse thee.
x.KJV: Because they met you not with bread and with water in the way, when ye came forth out of Egypt; and because they hired against thee Balaam the son of Beor of Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse thee.
x.YLT: because that they have not come before you with bread and with water in the way, in your coming out from Egypt, and because he hath hired against thee Balaam son of Beor, of Pethor of Aram-Naharaim, to revile thee;

nt: The phrase **on account of the matter that** introduces the reasons for God’s command that the Ammonites and Moabites could not enter the assembly of Yahweh. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a connecting word or phrase that shows that the information that follows gives the reasons for the prohibition that came before. Alternate translation: [because]
The word **you** is plural here, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **bread and water** represent food and drink in general. Moses uses these basic items to refer to all the provisions that travelers would need. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with provisions] or [with the food and drink you needed]
The words **Balaam** and **Beor** are the names of men. Balaam was a prophet, and Beor was his father.
The name **Aram Naharaim** means “Aram of the two rivers” (Euphrates and Tigris) and is in the region later called “Mesopotamia.”

Here, **to curse you** marks this phrase as the goal or purpose of the Ammonites and Moabites hiring Balaam. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to curse you] or [with the intention of cursing you]

x.ASV: Nevertheless Jehovah thy God would not hearken unto Balaam; but Jehovah thy God turned the curse into a blessing unto thee, because Jehovah thy God loved thee.
x.Darby: But Jehovah thyGod would not listen to Balaam; and Jehovah thyGod turned the curse into blessing unto thee, because Jehovah thyGod loved thee.
x.KJV: Nevertheless the Lord thy God would not hearken unto Balaam; but the Lord thy God turned the curse into a blessing unto thee, because the Lord thy God loved thee.
x.YLT: and Jehovah thy God hath not been willing to hearken unto Balaam, and Jehovah thy God doth turn for thee the reviling to a blessing, because Jehovah thy God hath loved thee;

nt: וְ⁠לֹֽא־אָבָ֞ה יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֣עַ אֶל־בִּלְעָ֔ם וַ⁠יַּהֲפֹךְ֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֧י⁠ךָ לְּ⁠ךָ֛ אֶת־הַ⁠קְּלָלָ֖ה לִ⁠בְרָכָ֑ה כִּ֥י אֲהֵֽבְ⁠ךָ֖ יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽי⁠ךָ

The word **because** introduces the reason for what came before. If it would be clearer in your language, you could reverse the order and put the reason first. Alternate translation: [Yahweh your God loved you, so he was not willing to listen to Balaam and turned the curse into a blessing for you]
יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ & יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֧י⁠ךָ & יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽי⁠ךָ
See how you translated the phrase “Yahweh your God” in [1:10](../01/10.md).

Moses uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the Ammonites’ and Moabites’ intention to curse Israel and Yahweh’s refusal to allow it. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, Yahweh your God was not willing to listen to Balaam]

By **was not willing to listen to Balaam**, Moses means “would not do what Balaam said.” See the discussion of “listen” in the Introduction to Deuteronomy for further information about this. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh your God would not do what Balaam asked] or [But Yahweh your God refused to do what Balaam wanted]
וַ⁠יַּהֲפֹךְ֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֧י⁠ךָ לְּ⁠ךָ֛ אֶת־הַ⁠קְּלָלָ֖ה לִ⁠בְרָכָ֑ה

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **curse** and **blessing**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh your God changed what would have harmed you into what helped you]

x.ASV: Thou shalt not seek their peace nor their prosperity all thy days for ever.
x.Darby: Thou shalt not seek their peace nor their prosperity all thy days for ever.
x.KJV: Thou shalt not seek their peace nor their prosperity all thy days for ever.
x.YLT: thou dost not seek their peace and their good all thy days--to the age.

nt: Moses is referring to any good things by naming two major components, **peace** and **prosperity**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their well-being] or [anything good for them]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **peace** and **prosperity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [for them to live peacefully or to prosper]

Moses is using **all your days, to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “continuously throughout all time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all time to come] or [perpetually]

x.ASV: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a sojourner in his land.
x.Darby: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother. Thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a sojourner in his land.
x.KJV: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land.
x.YLT: `Thou dost not abominate an Edomite, for thy brother he is; thou dost not abominate an Egyptian, for a sojourner thou hast been in his land;

nt: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [You shall not detest an Edomite because he is your brother]

Here Moses is speaking of an Edomite as if he were actually a **brother** to an Israelite. He means that the Edomites were descendants of Esau, who was the brother of Jacob, the ancestor of the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for he comes from our relative Esau]

The word **because** introduces the reason for the command not to detest Egyptians. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since you were foreigners in the land of Egypt, do not detest the Egyptians]

x.ASV: The children of the third generation that are born unto them shall enter into the assembly of Jehovah.
x.Darby: Children that are born to them shall come into the congregation of Jehovah in the third generation.

nt: Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [descendants that are born to them] or [children that are born to them]

The expression **are born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The sons who become part of their families] or [The sons who come from their families]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **the third generation**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [after three generations]

Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [who becomes unclean because of something that happens while he sleeps] or [who has a bodily discharge during the night]

x.Darby: For Jehovah thyGod walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee; and thy camp shall be holy, that he see nothing unseemly with thee, and turn away from thee.

nt: **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. This verse gives the reason for all the instructions about cleanliness in verses 1–13. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before.

Here Moses is speaking of **Yahweh** walking **in the midst of your camp** as if God were physically moving around in the Israelite camp. This image represents God’s active presence with his people and his close involvement in their affairs. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh your God is present among you in your camp] or [Yahweh your God is actively watching over you in your camp]

Here, **to give you victory and to give your enemies to your faces** marks the goal or purpose of **Yahweh your God walks in the midst of your camp**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to make you victorious and to deliver your enemies into your power]

The phrase **to your faces** represents “into your power” or “into your presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and to give your enemies into your power] or [and to deliver your enemies to you]

Moses is using the phrase **and turn away from you** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the Israelites an instruction to keep their camp holy so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [or else he will turn away from you] or [lest he turn away from you]

Moses is using **as good to him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “as he pleases” or “wherever he wants.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. x.ASV: There shall be no prostitute of the daughters of Israel, neither shall there be a sodomite of the sons of Israel.
x.Darby: There shall be no prostitute amongst the daughters of Israel, nor any Sodomite amongst the sons of Israel.

x.YLT: `There is not a whore among the daughters of Israel, nor is there a whoremonger among the sons of Israel;

nt: The term **cultic prostitute** refers to someone who engaged in sexual acts as part of the worship of pagan gods. This practice was common in ancient Canaanite religion but was forbidden in Israel. If your readers would not be familiar with what a cultic prostitute is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [woman who performs sexual acts in pagan worship … man who performs sexual acts in pagan worship] or [female temple prostitute who serves false gods … male temple prostitute who serves false gods]

Here Moses is using the term **brother** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.
